opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think smooth fundraising made it easier for me to avoid hard truths, and I didn't fully realize that until later.

When we started Taichi Graphics, raising money went surprisingly well. Investors were excited about the technology, and there was a lot of enthusiasm for the open-source project and for developer tools in general. When money comes in that easily, you start to take it as validation. You think, "Smart people are betting on us, so we must be on the right track." That feeling is very comfortable, and it's dangerous.

The harsh reality for a lot of infrastructure companies, including ours, is that a great open-source project with stars and an excited community isn't the same as a business. Who exactly is paying, how much, and why do they need you instead of something else? Those are the questions you should be obsessing over from day one. With a lot of money in the bank, there's no external pressure forcing you to answer them. You can hire more people, build more features, polish the technology, and it all feels like progress.

Looking back, I was a researcher at heart. I loved the technical problems, and the funding gave me room to keep living in that world a bit longer than I should have. If fundraising had been harder, I think I would have been pushed earlier to talk to customers, cut things that weren't working, and make painful decisions about focus.

So my lesson is that easy money doesn't remove problems, it just postpones when you have to face them, and they usually get bigger in the meantime. Now I try to act as if the money were scarce even when it isn't. I ask myself: if we couldn't raise another round, what would we do differently tomorrow? Whatever the answer is, that's probably what we should be doing anyway.

r001.rationale: The response says that having money in the bank removed external pressure to confront business realities, and that easy money postponed facing problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, smooth fundraising made me worse at it. When money comes easily, it feels like external validation that everything you're doing is right, and that's a dangerous signal to trust.

At Taichi, we raised quickly. Investors were excited about the technology, about the open-source community, about the team. And I remember feeling like every round closing was proof that we had figured it out. But fundraising success measures how compelling your story is to investors. It doesn't measure whether customers actually need what you're building, or whether you have a repeatable way to make money.

The problem is that when the bank account is full, the harsh questions become optional. You can tell yourself, "We'll figure out monetization next year." You can keep investing in the parts you love, which for me was the compiler and the technology itself, and postpone the uncomfortable conversation about whether the market is really there. Runway becomes a cushion that lets you avoid pain, rather than a tool for buying time to find the truth.

In hindsight, I wish we had treated a successful round as the start of the hard questions, not the end of them. Something like: "Okay, we have thirty months. What's the one thing that has to be true for this business to work, and how fast can we prove or disprove it?" Instead, the comfort delayed that reckoning by probably a year or more.

The lesson I took away is that confronting reality is a discipline, not something circumstances force on you. If your circumstances are good, you actually have to work harder at it, because nothing external is pushing you to look.

r001.rationale: He says a full bank account made harsh questions optional and that the resulting comfort delayed the reckoning by a year or more, conveying that the lack of immediate financial pressure postponed confronting reality.

astra-6.text: I think smooth fundraising made it easier for me to avoid confronting hard problems. When investors keep supporting you, you can start treating that as evidence that the company is doing well. But raising money and building something customers really need are different things. With enough money in the bank, I could tell myself we just needed more time or more people, instead of asking whether our assumptions were wrong. So it reduced the urgency to face reality, even though that was exactly what I needed to do.

r001.rationale: The response says smooth fundraising and having enough money reduced the urgency to face reality, making it easier to avoid hard problems.
